system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-02-28 01:15:00 to 2174-03-02 14:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with left-sided abdominal pain and a history of diarrhea, concerning for diverticulitis, in the setting of neutropenia due to recent Revlimid therapy for relapsed multiple myeloma. A CT scan confirmed mild diverticulitis, and he was treated with five days of IV meropenem and fluconazole, followed by oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. He was made NPO initially due to infection risk but advanced to a full diet as symptoms resolved. His neutropenia was managed with Neupogen, resulting in improved white blood cell count. His INR was supratherapeutic on admission, requiring temporary hold and subsequent dose reduction of warfarin. A new nonocclusive deep vein thrombosis in the right femoral and popliteal veins was identified, and anticoagulation was continued. Revlimid was held during hospitalization due to infection risk. He improved clinically, remained afebrile, and was discharged home on oral antibiotics, adjusted warfarin, and home medications with follow-up arranged in hematology, rectal clinic, and anticoagulation clinic.
problems: Diverticulitis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
Multiple myeloma, without mention of having achieved remission
Peripheral stem cells replaced by transplant
Acute venous embolism and thrombosis of other specified veins
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Unspecified hereditary and idiopathic peripheral neuropathy
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of prostate

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Multiple myeloma on immunosuppression with diarrhea.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric CT imaging was performed through the abdomen and pelvis
with oral contrast only, IV contrast was not administered for the exam.  Post
processing performed in the coronal and sagittal planes.

COMPARISON:  CT from ___.

FINDINGS:

Abdomen:  The liver, gallbladder, spleen, adrenal glands, and pancreas are
normal in noncontrast appearance.  There is a punctate nonobstructing calculus
in the right lower pole renal collecting system.  The kidneys are otherwise
normal in appearance.  The small bowel and proximal large bowel are within
normal limits aside from scattered colonic diverticula.  There is no
significant mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  There are
atherosclerotic changes of the abdominal aorta.  There is a stable compression
deformity of the T12 vertebral body.  No acute osseous abnormalities are seen.

Pelvis:  There is persistent abnormal thickening in the distal descending and
sigmoid colon.  This appears slightly improved compared to prior exam.  The
surrounding inflammatory changes seen on the previous CT have also decreased. 
There is no evidence of extraluminal fluid collection to suggest abscess or
perforation.  The patient is status post prostatectomy.  The bladder wall
appears stably mildly thickened.  There is a 2.9 x 1.4 cm cystic structure
marginating the left superior pubic ramus which is favored to represent a
benign postoperative fluid collection such as a lymphocele.  There is no
significant pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  The osseous structures are
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

Persistent abnormal thickening of the distal descending and sigmoid colon
compared to the prior CT in ___.  The degree of thickening and
surrounding inflammatory change appears mildly improved when compared to the
prior study.  Findings may represent a slowly resolving diverticulitis or
colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___. You came in with nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I started feeling nauseous yesterday, then I vomited a few times. I haven’t been able to keep anything down. I feel weak and dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, abdominal pain, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, and no belly pain. I did have one episode of diarrhea at home. My wife checked my temperature—it was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of multiple myeloma and being on Revlimid, we have to be careful with infections. We’ve started you on IV fluids and gave you Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t been taking my Revlimid the past few days because I felt so sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to know. We’ll hold it for now and restart when your oncologist approves. Your labs show low white blood cells—ANC is 1100—so you’re somewhat immunocompromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this could be an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re treating it as a gastrointestinal infection. We’ve started antibiotics—Cipro and Flagyl—just in case, especially since you’re immunocompromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on those before. Are they safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. They’re safe. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen to rule out anything serious like a bowel issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s some thickening in the lower part of your colon, which could be from mild diverticulitis or colitis. But it looks like it’s improving compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before. Is it acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it’s not severe. We think your current symptoms are more from a viral or bacterial GI infection, maybe with some reactive joint pain—you mentioned your joints hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my knees and shoulders ache. I also had a runny nose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with a viral syndrome. We’ve ruled out pneumonia, stroke, and heart issues with normal chest X-ray, CT head, and cardiac markers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my blood thinner? I take warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was high—3.3—so we held your warfarin temporarily. An ultrasound showed a non-occlusive clot in your right leg veins, which we’ve seen before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the same clot? Not worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s not blocking blood flow. We’ll restart warfarin at 5 mg tonight and monitor your INR closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and other common bacteria. No parasites either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may not find a specific organism. Given your symptoms and immune status, we’re continuing the antibiotics as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’m feeling a bit better—less nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep you on IV fluids today and transition to oral intake as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs today show stable hemoglobin, and your white count is still low but not worsening. We’re continuing the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on my hepatitis B? I’m on lamivudine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HBV DNA is undetectable—great news. You’re doing well on lamivudine. We’ll keep you on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes—my sugars been okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose has been stable. You’re on your usual insulin—glargine at night and sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my neuropathy—can I keep taking gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re adjusting the dose. You’ll take 100 mg in the morning, 100 mg in the afternoon, and 200 mg at night. It’s safer with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. You’ve improved, your nausea is gone, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual meds. Take warfarin 5 mg tonight, then 3 mg daily. Get your INR checked in a few days and call your PCP with the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full 7-day course—Cipro twice daily, Flagyl three times daily. Call your oncologist to restart Revlimid after you finish antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—fever, vomiting, shortness of breath, leg swelling, or chest pain. If any of those happen, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your primary doctor and oncologist soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with nausea, vomiting, and dehydration in the setting of multiple myeloma and immunocompromise. He had not taken his Revlimid recently and presented with symptoms suggestive of a gastrointestinal infection, possibly viral or bacterial, with reactive joint pain. Workup included negative CT head and chest X-ray, and CT abdomen showed persistent but improved colonic thickening, likely from resolving diverticulitis or colitis. Stool studies were negative for pathogens. He was treated with IV fluids, Ciprofloxacin, and Metronidazole for presumed gastroenteritis. His supratherapeutic INR of 3.3 led to a temporary hold on warfarin, with resumption at 5 mg nightly; ultrasound confirmed a non-occlusive DVT in the right femoral and popliteal veins. He improved clinically, remained afebrile, and was discharged home on oral antibiotics, adjusted warfarin, and home medications with instructions to follow up with his PCP and oncologist.
